title: Framework Laptop 13 Pro review: Much better battery, much worse price
excerpt: Framework's latest modular laptop trades one set of problems for another.
content_html:
right laptop, wrong time

Framework’s latest modular laptop trades one set of problems for another.

Credit: Andrew Cunningham

Credit: Andrew Cunningham

I’ve liked the Framework Laptop 13 since the first time I used it, partly because I just think the idea of a repairable and upgradeable laptop is cool and partly because it’s not Yet Another Ultraportable Trying To Be A MacBook Air Clone. But the design has always had real shortcomings—the most noticeable and serious being its mediocre battery life.

Enter the Framework Laptop 13 Pro. While all previous Laptop 13 refreshes have tinkered around the edges with the original design (a tweaked lid design here, new hinges or new speakers there), the Laptop 13 Pro is as close as we’ve gotten to a second-generation revision for the original design.

This means that it breaks backward compatibility for some (but not all) Laptop 13 components, most notably the bottom case, the keyboard and trackpad, and the original 55 WHr and 61 WHr battery designs. But by allowing itself to make larger changes to the design, Framework has made major strides in battery life and general fit and finish.

The result is Framework’s nicest-looking, nicest-feeling, most polished laptop design. It’s also possible for existing Laptop 13 users to get some or all of its benefits by retrofitting their laptops with new parts. That’s good because the Laptop 13 Pro is also quite expensive, even by 2026’s ridiculous standards for consumer tech—no model costs less than $1,500, and you’d spend nearly $3,000 to get the version I was sent for review.

Design changes

The Laptop 13 Pro looks a lot like the regular Framework Laptop 13, but with a new “Graphite” finish. Andrew Cunningham

The first thing you’ll notice about the Laptop 13 Pro is that it has traded in Framework’s traditional, more industrial-looking silver for an anodized dark gray “graphite” finish. On the “dark-finished aluminum” spectrum, it’s about as dark as Apple’s Midnight finish but without the same bluish tint; it does attract fingerprints in a similar way, though. Framework is offering Laptop 13 Pro parts in the original aluminum finish, but they are primarily intended for original Framework Laptop owners who are buying upgrades.

Framework says that the Laptop 13 Pro is its first to be “fully machined out of extruded blocks of 6063 aluminum,” and as a result, the device’s body feels slightly more solid and substantial than the original version.

The redesigned bottom case allowed Framework to fit in a bigger battery than older Laptop 13 models—74 WHr, up from 61 WHr in previous models and 55 WHr in the first couple generations. The release mechanism for the expansion modules has also been changed. The original Laptop 13 had buttons that had to be continually pressed as you pried the expansion modules out; the Laptop 13 Pro uses the same kind of on/off retention switches Framework uses in the Laptop 16 and Laptop 12.

The keyboard’s look and feel hasn’t changed much from previous generations, but it now comes in versions with either lavender or orange/gray keycap highlights. The trackpad changes more noticeably; in part to make room for the bigger battery, Framework has shifted from a trackpad with a physical clicking mechanism to a haptic trackpad that uses vibrations to simulate clicking. It’s a change Apple made in most of its laptops a decade or so ago, and the situation is similar here: it’s different, and it’s not quite as tactile as a “real” click. But with the firmness turned all the way up, it’s close enough, and it’s nice to get the same response no matter where you click on the trackpad.

The final change of note is to the screen, which keeps the same size (13.5 inches), resolution (2,880×1,920), aspect ratio (3:2), refresh rate (30 to 120 Hz), and panel type (IPS) but also includes touch support. This is Framework’s first touchscreen display, but even if you don’t care about touch support, you might like the other quality-of-life improvements: a 700 nit “typical brightness,” a 1,800:1 contrast ratio, and an updated anti-glare coating.

Those are all marginal but noticeable improvements over the previous-generation display, and if you’re still using a glossy or matte 2,256×1,504 screen from early Framework Laptop 13 iterations, this new screen will be an especially noticeable upgrade. But it’s still not an OLED display, and it’s still missing complete coverage of the DCI-P3 color gamut, to name a couple of more advanced features that remain absent. And the display quality still isn’t perfect; I noticed minor light bleed across the top of my review unit’s display when it was showing something dark.

(One less-noticeable screen change: the top corners of the new screen are actual 90-degree angles again, rather than little curves. The curves on the older display were a side effect of a display panel Framework used that was originally designed for another company. The corners never really bothered me that much, and I hesitate to call this an “upgrade” in and of itself. But the rounded corners didn’t line up with Framework’s bezels, and Windows and Linux have never respected the tiny little dead zones that they create, so, sure, fine.)

In the end, this is still the Framework Laptop 13. But it’s probably as close to a design overhaul as you can get while still maintaining compatibility with a critical mass of important parts (the board, screen, and expansion port modules chief among them).

“The MacBook Pro for Linux users”

Framework is positioning the Laptop 13 Pro as a “MacBook Pro for Linux users,” and Ubuntu 24.04 LTS is available for the first time as a preinstalled OS for the laptop’s prebuilt edition.

The Laptop 13 Pro still supports Windows 11 just fine, of course, and for the sake of consistency, all of my performance and battery benchmarks were done in Windows 11 25H2.

But aside from the ability to have Linux preinstalled, there’s actually nothing special about the Laptop 13 Pro’s Linux support. That’s because Framework has officially supported Ubuntu and Fedora on all of its laptops, including previous Laptop 13 models. After a couple of bumpy years during which Linux users who wanted BIOS updates would need to figure out how to temporarily install Windows first, Framework’s BIOS updates are available for easy download and installation through LVFS (the Ryzen 7040 version of the Framework Laptop that I run Kubuntu 26.04 on, for example, grabbed its Laptop 13 Pro-supporting BIOS update through the same updater as all other apps and system components).

Apart from Ubuntu 24.04, Framework says that Ubuntu 26.04 LTS and Fedora 44 are officially supported and should work out of the box, while CachyOS, Bazzite, Arch, and NixOS 26.05 are all “compatible community supported distributions” that will generally work fine with a little extra tweaking. Any distribution you run should include at least Linux kernel version 6.19 to ensure working support for Intel’s Core Ultra Series 3 chips and the rest of Framework’s hardware; kernel 7.0 or higher is recommended.

The agony and the ecstasy of LPCAMM memory modules

Another major design change is internal. After a few generations of boards that used DDR5 SO-DIMMs, the Core Ultra Series 3 board has switched to LPDDR5X memory in the LPCAMM2 form factor.

If you haven’t heard of LPCAMM2 before, here are the basics: CAMM stands for Compression-Attached Memory Module. Where SO-DIMMs have copper contacts across the bottom edge that go into a slot, CAMM has copper contacts spread across one entire side. The RAM and a small piece of aluminum are both held in place with screws that press the RAM module’s copper contacts down against contacts on the motherboard; the metal piece works as both a heat spreader and shielding that protects the rest of the components from electromagnetic interference. (Framework’s blog says the shielding contributes to a major improvement in wireless performance for the Laptop 13 Pro). The Laptop 13 Pro uses just a single LPCAMM2 module; there’s no need to use matched pairs of RAM modules to get dual-channel memory speeds, as you have to do with DDR4 or DDR5 DIMMs and SO-DIMMs.

The shift to LPCAMM2 comes with real benefits; the “LP” in both LPCAMM2 and LPDDR5X stands for “low-power,” making the RAM change one of several factors contributing to improved battery life in the Laptop 13 Pro. LPDDR5X also supports higher memory speeds than regular DDR5 SO-DIMMs do (though it’s still apparently easier to support faster speeds with soldered-down, non-upgradeable memory).

But moving to LPCAMM2 was also something of a necessity for Framework. The company doesn’t seem to want to ship a laptop with non-upgradeable memory, as it had to use in the Framework Desktop (Framework didn’t ship a Core Ultra Series 2 laptop at all, possibly because the most suitable processors from that chip family used RAM that was integrated into the CPU package). But it also had to use LPDDR5X to ship the higher-end Core Ultra Series 3 processors and their fully enabled Intel Arc integrated GPUs. Unlike the past Intel and AMD generations Framework has used, regular DDR5 isn’t even supported. That makes LPCAMM2 the only real option, bleeding edge though it is.

Framework isn’t the first laptop manufacturer to use LPCAMM2. Both Dell and Lenovo have experimented with the modules in a couple of laptops so far. But it’s rare, and in the short term, that rarity makes it harder to buy, both for end users and for Framework itself. Framework has been increasing prices for various components all year as shortages of RAM and other components have dragged on, but its supplier recently doubled the prices Framework was paying for LPCAMM2 modules, an increase Framework will be passing on to most people who haven’t already put in their Laptop 13 Pro preorders.

So going with LPCAMM2 is double-edged: it is both technically beneficial and technically necessary, but it’s also singlehandedly driving up the price of an already pretty expensive boutique-y laptop. It’s not Framework’s fault, but it is Framework’s reality, and it’s too bad that such a high price will make this laptop’s improvements mostly theoretical, even to people who could pay the prices Framework was charging a couple of years ago.

Upgrading an older Laptop 13

Some Laptop 13 Pro parts break compatibility with the older Framework Laptop 13, but Framework did manage to preserve compatibility between many major components. That means older Laptop 13 models can benefit from newer Laptop 13 Pro parts—the same as any of the other upgraded boards Framework has released for the Laptop 13 over the years—and that the new Laptop Pro chassis can be built around older, cheaper Framework motherboards.

If you’re looking for an easy rule of thumb, treat the new 74 WHr battery, input cover with the haptic trackpad, and bottom case as a single upgrade. If you want the benefits of any of these components, you need to buy all of them. You can’t just put the new battery into an existing Framework Laptop 13, and you can’t use the new input cover with the old battery and bottom cover.

But motherboards, displays, and USB-C expansion cards are all interchangeable between the Laptop 13 and the Laptop 13 Pro. If you just want to buy a new Core Ultra Series 3 motherboard and put it in your existing Laptop 13, you can (along with a new CAMM memory module, of course). If you want to keep all of your current parts but upgrade to the new-and-improved touchscreen display panel, you can.

Here’s a non-comprehensive table listing the current prices for some of the upgrades for current Laptop 13 owners who want to benefit from some of the Laptop 13 Pro’s improvements without springing for a full-priced upgrade. Bear in mind that many of these parts are listed on Framework’s site but are either out of stock or have not yet been made available to purchase. Buyers can “register interest” in an all-in-one upgrade kit that includes a new battery, keyboard, and bottom case for an original Laptop 13, but it’s not available to buy yet, either.

I’ve tested various combinations of new and old components, with a particular interest in figuring out how much of the Laptop 13 Pro’s massively improved battery life can be chalked up to the larger battery and how much is only possible because of the new Core Ultra Series 3 motherboard.

It’s a mark of how far Framework has come in the last few years that this kind of testing is even possible. The last time the company bumped up its battery capacity, it was months (and months) before some motherboards got finalized BIOS updates that added compatibility for the new hardware. Now, all versions of the Framework Laptop 13 board, going all the way back to the original 11th-generation Intel Core board, already have updated firmware with the new hardware support locked and loaded. Update to the latest BIOS version before you make the move, and any Framework board can become Pro.

Performance and battery life

Framework uses Intel’s Core Ultra Series 3 chips (codenamed Panther Lake), which are Intel’s best laptop processors in quite a while. They offer a combination of CPU performance, GPU performance, and power efficiency that makes them a great all-around upgrade for any Intel-based Laptop 13 owner, though the Ryzen AI 300-series board does usually keep performance close-ish.

I tested the Core Ultra X7 358H version of the laptop. Framework lists a faster Core Ultx X9 388H version, but it’s a “limited batch” configuration that hasn’t actually been available to preorder for a while. That’s fine, though—the Core Ultra X7 358H has the same CPU and GPU core counts and is much faster than the Core Ultra 5 325 base model, so you aren’t missing out on much if you can’t get the X9 version.

Nothing about the Laptop 13’s performance is too surprising if you’ve already seen what Panther Lake is capable of, though Framework sets the X7 358H’s sustained power limits at a relatively tame 30 W (in Windows’ Best Performance preset mode) and 25 W (in Balanced mode). That means that in sustained CPU and GPU-heavy tasks like video encoding and gaming, the Laptop 13 Pro isn’t capable of the same heights as the Asus Zenbook UX8407, partly because it used the Core Ultra X9 chip but mostly because it had a higher sustained power limit of 55 W.

Where Panther Lake really helps the Laptop 13 Pro shine is in battery life. In the PCMark 10 Modern Office test with the screen brightness set to 200 nits, the Laptop 13 Pro and its 74 WHr battery lasted for just a hair over 18 hours, far more than any previous Framework Laptop 13 and finally long enough to decisively eliminate “mediocre-to-poor battery life” as the laptop’s biggest downside.

We also did some limited testing with other Framework parts to see how the 74 WHr battery would perform with older Framework boards and how the Core Ultra Series 3 board would perform if it were dropped into a current Framework Laptop 13 with a 61 WHr battery.

Maybe unsurprisingly, the vast majority of the Laptop 13 Pro’s battery life can be attributed to the Panther Lake chip and LPCAMM2 memory. Paired with the 61 WHr Framework battery, the board still managed to last for around 15 hours and 45 minutes. That means upgraders will get a substantial battery life boost from upgrading the board, even if they don’t spring for the new bottom case, keyboard cover, and 74 WHr battery combo.

When testing the Ryzen AI 300 version of the Framework Laptop board with the new 74 WHr battery, we got just over 11 hours of runtime, compared to around 8.5 hours with the 61 WHr battery. That’s a noticeable improvement, but it’s also essentially proportionate to the capacity increase. The upgrade is especially worth pursuing if you’re still using one of the old (and aging) 55 WHr Framework batteries, but it’s not as significant as the board upgrade.

The right refresh at the wrong time

Framework has been unusually public about its component struggles this year, partly because the company has always been a bit more transparent about its operations than other PC makers and partly to try to defuse criticism of its steady drumbeat of price increases.

The unfortunate truth is that this is simultaneously Framework’s best, most interesting board upgrade ever and also one that’s priced so high because of the RAM crisis and other component shortages that it’s often difficult to make any kind of purchase make sense. A 32GB stick of LPCAMM2 costs $800 from Framework’s site; one of the few available aftermarket sticks is $700. Even by the standards of the RAM shortage, that’s a steep asking price.

For existing Framework Laptop owners looking for upgrades, some of the new parts are somewhat easier to justify, which is one thing Framework can boast that most laptop makers can’t. It still costs a few hundred dollars, but you can keep the specs you have now and benefit from a larger battery and a better-built bottom case for a fraction of the price of an all-new machine.

For anyone else, the situation is murkier. It’s hard to know how the current component shortages will resolve—will things even out and prices come back down over the next year or two, or will you look back on our current awful pricing landscape and wish you’d bought something before things got even worse? Either way, there are good laptops you can buy for a lot less than this, including the actual MacBook Pro.

The good

  • Typical Framework benefits: modular, repairable, upgradeable design; nice screen, keyboard, and trackpad; official support for both Linux and Windows.
  • Great battery life that finally addresses one of the Framework Laptop 13’s biggest shortcomings.
  • A nice balance of CPU and GPU performance.
  • Improved build quality.
  • Some part compatibility between this and the original Framework Laptop 13.

The bad

  • Expensive.
  • Battery, keyboard cover, and bottom case are incompatible with the original Laptop 13. If you want to upgrade any of them, you have to upgrade all of them.
  • Customizable ports, but you still get only four of them.

The ugly

  • Framework has switched to an exotic new upgradeable LPDDR5X RAM format just in time for those modules to become astronomically expensive.

Andrew is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica, with a focus on consumer tech including computer hardware and in-depth reviews of operating systems like Windows and macOS. Andrew lives in Philadelphia and co-hosts a weekly book podcast called Overdue.

Where Panther Lake really helps the Laptop 13 Pro shine is in battery life. In the PCMark 10 Modern Office test with the screen brightness set to 200 nits, the Laptop 13 Pro and its 74 WHr battery lasted for just a hair over 18 hours, far more than any previous Framework Laptop 13 and finally long enough to decisively eliminate “mediocre-to-poor battery life” as the laptop’s biggest downside. We also did some limited testing with other Framework parts to see how the 74 WHr battery would perform with older Framework boards and how the Core Ultra Series 3 board would perform if it were dropped into a current Framework Laptop 13 with a 61 WHr battery. Maybe unsurprisingly, the vast majority of the Laptop 13 Pro’s battery life can be attributed to the Panther Lake chip and LPCAMM2 memory. Paired with the 61 WHr Framework battery, the board still managed to last for around 15 hours and 45 minutes. That means upgraders will get a substantial battery life boost from upgrading the board, even if they don’t spring for the new bottom case, keyboard cover, and 74 WHr battery combo. When testing the Ryzen AI 300 version of the Framework Laptop board with the new 74 WHr battery, we got just over 11 hours of runtime, compared to around 8.5 hours with the 61 WHr battery. That’s a noticeable improvement, but it’s also essentially proportionate to the capacity increase. The upgrade is especially worth pursuing if you’re still using one of the old (and aging) 55 WHr Framework batteries, but it’s not as significant as the board upgrade. The right refresh at the wrong time Framework has been unusually public about its component struggles this year, partly because the company has always been a bit more transparent about its operations than other PC makers and partly to try to defuse criticism of its steady drumbeat of price increases. The unfortunate truth is that this is simultaneously Framework’s best, most interesting board upgrade ever and also one that’s priced so high because of the RAM crisis and other component shortages that it’s often difficult to make any kind of purchase make sense. A 32GB stick of LPCAMM2 costs $800 from Framework’s site; one of the few available aftermarket sticks is $700. Even by the standards of the RAM shortage, that’s a steep asking price. For existing Framework Laptop owners looking for upgrades, some of the new parts are somewhat easier to justify, which is one thing Framework can boast that most laptop makers can’t. It still costs a few hundred dollars, but you can keep the specs you have now and benefit from a larger battery and a better-built bottom case for a fraction of the price of an all-new machine. For anyone else, the situation is murkier. It’s hard to know how the current component shortages will resolve—will things even out and prices come back down over the next year or two, or will you look back on our current awful pricing landscape and wish you’d bought something before things got even worse? Either way, there are good laptops you can buy for a lot less than this, including the actual MacBook Pro. The good Typical Framework benefits: modular, repairable, upgradeable design; nice screen, keyboard, and trackpad; official support for both Linux and Windows. Great battery life that finally addresses one of the Framework Laptop 13’s biggest shortcomings. A nice balance of CPU and GPU performance. Improved build quality. Some part compatibility between this and the original Framework Laptop 13. The bad Expensive. Battery, keyboard cover, and bottom case are incompatible with the original Laptop 13. If you want to upgrade any of them, you have to upgrade all of them. Customizable ports, but you still get only four of them. The ugly Framework has switched to an exotic new upgradeable LPDDR5X RAM format just in time for those modules to become astronomically expensive. Andrew is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica, with a focus on consumer tech including computer hardware and in-depth reviews of operating systems like Windows and macOS. Andrew lives in Philadelphia and co-hosts a weekly book podcast called Overdue. 75 Comments

sentences.en: The agony and the ecstasy of LPCAMM memory modules

blocks.html_en: Another major design change is internal. After a few generations of boards that used DDR5 SO-DIMMs, the Core Ultra Series 3 board has switched to LPDDR5X memory in the LPCAMM2 form factor.

sentences.en: Another major design change is internal.

sentences.en: After a few generations of boards that used DDR5 SO-DIMMs, the Core Ultra Series 3 board has switched to LPDDR5X memory in the LPCAMM2 form factor.

blocks.html_en: If you haven’t heard of LPCAMM2 before, here are the basics: CAMM stands for Compression-Attached Memory Module. Where SO-DIMMs have copper contacts across the bottom edge that go into a slot, CAMM has copper contacts spread across one entire side. The RAM and a small piece of aluminum are both held in place with screws that press the RAM module’s copper contacts down against contacts on the motherboard; the metal piece works as both a heat spreader and shielding that protects the rest of the components from electromagnetic interference. (Framework’s blog says the shielding contributes to a major improvement in wireless performance for the Laptop 13 Pro). The Laptop 13 Pro uses just a single LPCAMM2 module; there’s no need to use matched pairs of RAM modules to get dual-channel memory speeds, as you have to do with DDR4 or DDR5 DIMMs and SO-DIMMs.

blocks.html_en: The shift to LPCAMM2 comes with real benefits; the “LP” in both LPCAMM2 and LPDDR5X stands for “low-power,” making the RAM change one of several factors contributing to improved battery life in the Laptop 13 Pro. LPDDR5X also supports higher memory speeds than regular DDR5 SO-DIMMs do (though it’s still apparently easier to support faster speeds with soldered-down, non-upgradeable memory).

blocks.html_en: But moving to LPCAMM2 was also something of a necessity for Framework. The company doesn’t seem to want to ship a laptop with non-upgradeable memory, as it had to use in the Framework Desktop (Framework didn’t ship a Core Ultra Series 2 laptop at all, possibly because the most suitable processors from that chip family used RAM that was integrated into the CPU package). But it also had to use LPDDR5X to ship the higher-end Core Ultra Series 3 processors and their fully enabled Intel Arc integrated GPUs. Unlike the past Intel and AMD generations Framework has used, regular DDR5 isn’t even supported. That makes LPCAMM2 the only real option, bleeding edge though it is.

blocks.html_en: Framework isn’t the first laptop manufacturer to use LPCAMM2. Both Dell and Lenovo have experimented with the modules in a couple of laptops so far. But it’s rare, and in the short term, that rarity makes it harder to buy, both for end users and for Framework itself. Framework has been increasing prices for various components all year as shortages of RAM and other components have dragged on, but its supplier recently doubled the prices Framework was paying for LPCAMM2 modules, an increase Framework will be passing on to most people who haven’t already put in their Laptop 13 Pro preorders.

blocks.html_en: So going with LPCAMM2 is double-edged: it is both technically beneficial and technically necessary, but it’s also singlehandedly driving up the price of an already pretty expensive boutique-y laptop. It’s not Framework’s fault, but it is Framework’s reality, and it’s too bad that such a high price will make this laptop’s improvements mostly theoretical, even to people who could pay the prices Framework was charging a couple of years ago.

blocks.html_en: I’ve tested various combinations of new and old components, with a particular interest in figuring out how much of the Laptop 13 Pro’s massively improved battery life can be chalked up to the larger battery and how much is only possible because of the new Core Ultra Series 3 motherboard.

sentences.zh: 我测试了新旧组件的各种组合，特别想弄清楚 Laptop 13 Pro 电池寿命的大幅改善有多少可以归功于更大的电池，以及有多少只能归功于新的 Core Ultra Series 3 主板。

blocks.html_en: It’s a mark of how far Framework has come in the last few years that this kind of testing is even possible. The last time the company bumped up its battery capacity, it was months (and months) before some motherboards got finalized BIOS updates that added compatibility for the new hardware. Now, all versions of the Framework Laptop 13 board, going all the way back to the original 11th-generation Intel Core board, already have updated firmware with the new hardware support locked and loaded. blocks.html_en: Framework uses Intel’s Core Ultra Series 3 chips (codenamed Panther Lake), which are Intel’s best laptop processors in quite a while. content_html_zh:
正确的笔记本电脑，错误的时间

Framework 最新的模块化笔记本电脑解决了一系列问题。

图片来源：安德鲁·坎宁安

图片来源：安德鲁·坎宁安

自从我第一次使用 Framework Laptop 13 以来，我就很喜欢它，部分原因是我认为可修复和可升级笔记本电脑的想法很酷，部分原因是它不是又一款试图克隆 MacBook Air 的超便携笔记本电脑。 但该设计始终存在真正的缺点——最引人注目和最严重的是其平庸的电池寿命。

进入框架笔记本电脑 13 Pro。 虽然之前所有的 Laptop 13 更新都对原始设计的边缘进行了修改（这里调整了盖子设计，那里有新的铰链或新的扬声器），但 Laptop 13 Pro 已经最接近原始设计的第二代版本了。

这意味着它破坏了一些（但不是全部）Laptop 13 组件的向后兼容性，最明显的是底壳、键盘和触控板，以及原始的 55 WHr 和 61 WHr 电池设计。 但通过允许自己对设计进行更大的改变，Framework 在电池寿命和总体装配和表面处理方面取得了重大进步。

其结果是 Framework 的外观最漂亮、手感最好、最精致的笔记本电脑设计。 现有 Laptop 13 用户还可以通过使用新部件改装笔记本电脑来获得部分或全部好处。 这很好，因为 Laptop 13 Pro 也相当昂贵，即使按照 2026 年消费技术的荒谬标准，没有一款型号的价格低于 1,500 美元，而你要花近 3,000 美元才能得到我送审的版本。

设计变更

Laptop 13 Pro 看起来很像常规的 Framework Laptop 13，但采用了新的“石墨”饰面。 安德鲁坎宁安

关于 Laptop 13 Pro，您首先会注意到的是，它已经将 Framework 传统的、更具工业外观的银色换成了阳极氧化深灰色“石墨”饰面。 在“深色铝材”光谱中，它的颜色与苹果的午夜色差不多，但没有同样的蓝色色调；不过，它确实以类似的方式吸引指纹。 Framework 提供采用原始铝制饰面的 Laptop 13 Pro 部件，但它们主要面向购买升级的原始 Framework 笔记本电脑用户。

Framework 表示，Laptop 13 Pro 是首款“由 6063 铝挤压块完全加工而成”的笔记本电脑，因此，该设备的机身感觉比原始版本稍微更加坚固和坚固。

重新设计的底壳使 Framework 能够安装比旧款 Laptop 13 型号更大的电池 — 74 WHr，高于之前型号的 61 WHr 和前几代型号的 55 WHr。 扩展模块的释放机制也已更改。 最初的 Laptop 13 的按钮在您撬出扩展模块时必须连续按下； Laptop 13 Pro 使用与 Laptop 16 和 Laptop 12 Framework 相同类型的开/关保持开关。

键盘的外观和感觉与前几代相比没有太大变化，但现在有淡紫色或橙色/灰色键帽亮点的版本。 触控板的变化更加明显；部分是为了给更大的电池腾出空间，Framework 已从具有物理点击机制的触控板转变为使用振动来模拟点击的触觉触控板。 这是苹果公司大约十年前在其大多数笔记本电脑上做出的改变，这里的情况类似：它是不同的，而且它不像“真正的”点击那样有触觉。 但随着硬度一路调高，它已经足够接近了，而且无论您点击触控板的哪个位置，都能得到相同的响应，这真是太好了。

最后一个值得注意的变化是屏幕，它保持相同的尺寸（13.5英寸）、分辨率（2,880×1,920）、宽高比（3:2）、刷新率（30至120 Hz）和面板类型（IPS），但还包括触摸支持。 这是 Framework 的第一款触摸屏显示器，但即使您不关心触摸支持，您也可能会喜欢其他生活质量改进：700 尼特的“典型亮度”、1,800:1 的对比度和更新的防眩光涂层。

与上一代显示屏相比，这些都是微小但明显的改进，如果您仍在使用早期 Framework Laptop 13 迭代中的光面或磨砂 2,256×1,504 屏幕，那么这款新屏幕将是一个特别明显的升级。 但它仍然不是 OLED 显示屏，并且仍然无法完全覆盖 DCI-P3 色域，仅举几个仍然不存在的更高级功能。 而且显示质量仍然不完美；我注意到当我的评测设备的显示屏显示黑暗的东西时，它的顶部会出现轻微的漏光。

（一个不太明显的屏幕变化：新屏幕的顶角再次变为实际的 90 度角，而不是小曲线。 旧显示器上的曲线是最初为另一家公司设计的显示面板框架的副作用。 角落从来没有真正困扰过我，我犹豫是否称其为“升级”本身。 但圆角与 Framework 的边框不相符，Windows 和 Linux 从来不尊重它们创建的微小死区，所以，当然，很好。）

最终，这仍然是Framework Laptop 13。 但这可能是您所能得到的最接近的设计检修，同时仍然保持与大量重要部件（其中主要是主板、屏幕和扩展端口模块）的兼容性。

“适合 Linux 用户的 MacBook Pro”

Framework 将 Laptop 13 Pro 定位为“面向 Linux 用户的 MacBook Pro”，并且 Ubuntu 24.04 LTS 首次作为笔记本电脑预构建版本的预装操作系统提供。

当然，Laptop 13 Pro 仍然很好地支持 Windows 11，为了保持一致性，我所有的性能和电池基准测试都是在 Windows 11 25H2 中完成的。

但除了预装 Linux 的能力之外，Laptop 13 Pro 的 Linux 支持实际上没有什么特别的。 这是因为 Framework 已在其所有笔记本电脑上正式支持 Ubuntu 和 Fedora，包括之前的 Laptop 13 型号。 经过几年的坎坷，想要 BIOS 更新的 Linux 用户首先需要弄清楚如何临时安装 Windows，Framework 的 BIOS 更新可以通过 LVFS 轻松下载和安装（例如，我运行 Kubuntu 26.04 的 Framework 笔记本电脑的 Ryzen 7040 版本，通过与所有其他应用程序和系统组件相同的更新程序获取其支持笔记本电脑 13 Pro 的 BIOS 更新）。

除了 Ubuntu 24.04 之外，Framework 表示 Ubuntu 26.04 LTS 和 Fedora 44 都得到了官方支持，并且应该可以开箱即用，而 CachyOS、Bazzite、Arch 和 NixOS 26.05 都是“兼容的社区支持的发行版”，通常只需进行一些额外的调整就可以正常工作。 您运行的任何发行版都应至少包含 Linux 内核版本 6.19，以确保对英特尔 Core Ultra 系列 3 芯片和其余 Framework 硬件的工作支持；建议使用 7.0 或更高版本的内核。

LPCAMM 内存模块的痛苦与狂喜

另一个主要的设计变化是内部的。 在使用 DDR5 SO-DIMM 的几代主板之后，Core Ultra Series 3 主板已改用 LPCAMM2 外形规格的 LPDDR5X 内存。

如果您以前没有听说过 LPCAMM2，请了解以下基础知识：CAMM 代表压缩附加内存模块。 SO-DIMM 的铜触点分布在进入插槽的底部边缘，而 CAMM 的铜触点分布在整个一侧。 RAM 和一小块铝都用螺钉固定到位，螺钉将 RAM 模块的铜触点向下压在主板上的触点上；金属片既充当散热器又充当屏蔽层，保护其余组件免受电磁干扰。 （Framework 的博客称，屏蔽有助于大幅提高 Laptop 13 Pro 的无线性能）。 Laptop 13 Pro 仅使用一个 LPCAMM2 模块；无需使用匹配的 RAM 模块对来获得双通道内存速度，而您必须使用 DDR4 或 DDR5 DIMM 和 SO-DIMM。

转向 LPCAMM2 带来了真正的好处； LPCAMM2 和 LPDDR5X 中的“LP”代表“低功耗”，这使得 RAM 的改变成为有助于延长 Laptop 13 Pro 电池寿命的几个因素之一。 LPDDR5X 还支持比常规 DDR5 SO-DIMM 更高的内存速度（尽管使用焊接的、不可升级的内存显然仍然更容易支持更快的速度）。

但迁移到 LPCAMM2 对于 Framework 来说也是必要的。 该公司似乎不想提供带有不可升级内存的笔记本电脑，因为它必须在 Framework Desktop 中使用（Framework 根本没有提供 Core Ultra 系列 2 笔记本电脑，可能是因为该芯片系列中最合适的处理器使用集成到 CPU 封装中的 RAM）。 但它还必须使用 LPDDR5X 来交付更高端的 Core Ultra Series 3 处理器及其完全启用的 Intel Arc 集成 GPU。 与过去的 Intel 和 AMD 框架所使用的不同，常规 DDR5 甚至不受支持。 这使得 LPCAMM2 成为唯一真正的选择，尽管它很前沿。

Framework 并不是第一家使用 LPCAMM2 的笔记本电脑制造商。 到目前为止，戴尔和联想都已在几款笔记本电脑中试验了这些模块。 但它很罕见，而且在短期内，这种稀有性使得最终用户和框架本身都更难购买。 由于 RAM 和其他组件的短缺持续存在，Framework 全年都在提高各种组件的价格，但其供应商最近将 Framework 为 LPCAMM2 模块支付的价格提高了一倍，Framework 将把上涨的价格传递给大多数尚未预订 Laptop 13 Pro 的人。

因此，使用 LPCAMM2 是一把双刃剑：它既在技术上有利，又在技术上必要，但它也单独推高了本已相当昂贵的精品笔记本电脑的价格。 这不是 Framework 的错，但这是 Framework 的现实，而且太糟糕的是，如此高的价格将使这款笔记本电脑的改进主要停留在理论上，即使对于那些能够支付 Framework 几年前收取的价格的人来说也是如此。

升级旧笔记本电脑 13

某些 Laptop 13 Pro 部件破坏了与旧 Framework Laptop 13 的兼容性，但 Framework 确实设法保持了许多主要组件之间的兼容性。 这意味着较旧的 Laptop 13 型号可以受益于较新的 Laptop 13 Pro 部件（与 Framework 多年来为 Laptop 13 发布的任何其他升级主板相同），并且新的 Laptop Pro 机箱可以围绕较旧、更便宜的 Framework 主板构建。

如果您正在寻找简单的经验法则，请将新的 74 WHr 电池、带触觉触控板的输入盖和底壳视为一次升级。 如果您想享受其中任何组件的好处，则需要购买所有组件。 您不能将新电池直接放入现有的 Framework Laptop 13 中，也不能将新的输入盖与旧电池和底盖一起使用。

但主板、显示器和 USB-C 扩展卡在 Laptop 13 和 Laptop 13 Pro 之间都可以互换。 如果您只想购买新的 Core Ultra Series 3 主板并将其放入现有的 Laptop 13 中，则可以（当然还有新的 CAMM 内存模块）。 如果您想保留所有当前部件，但升级到新的和改进的触摸屏显示面板，您可以。

这是一个不全面的表格，列出了当前 Laptop 13 用户的一些升级的当前价格，他们希望从 Laptop 13 Pro 的一些改进中受益，而不需要全价升级。 请记住，其中许多部件都列在 Framework 网站上，但要么缺货，要么尚未可供购买。 买家可以对一款一体式升级套件“感兴趣”，其中包括原版 Laptop 13 的新电池、键盘和底壳，但目前还无法购买。

我测试了新旧组件的各种组合，特别想弄清楚 Laptop 13 Pro 电池寿命的大幅改善有多少可以归功于更大的电池，以及有多少只能归功于新的 Core Ultra Series 3 主板。

这标志着框架在过去几年中已经取得了多大的进步，这种测试甚至是可能的。 该公司上次提高电池容量时，是在几个月后，一些主板才完成 BIOS 更新，增加了对新硬件的兼容性。 现在，所有版本的 Framework Laptop 13 主板（一直到最初的第 11 代英特尔酷睿主板）都已经更新了固件，并锁定并加载了新的硬件支持。 在移动之前更新到最新的 BIOS 版本，任何 Framework 板都可以成为 Pro。

性能和电池寿命

Framework 使用英特尔的 Core Ultra 系列 3 芯片（代号为 Panther Lake），这是英特尔相当长一段时间以来最好的笔记本电脑处理器。 它们提供了 CPU 性能、GPU 性能和能效的组合，这使得它们成为任何基于 Intel 的 Laptop 13 用户的绝佳全面升级，尽管 Ryzen AI 300 系列主板通常会保持接近的性能。

我测试了Core Ultra X7 358H版本的笔记本电脑。 Framework 列出了更快的 Core Ultx X9 388H 版本，但它是“限量批量”配置，实际上已经有一段时间无法预订了。 不过没关系，Core Ultra X7 358H 具有相同的 CPU 和 GPU 核心数量，并且比 Core Ultra 5 325 基本型号快得多，因此如果您无法获得 X9 版本，您也不会错过太多东西。

如果您已经了解了 Panther Lake 的能力，那么 Laptop 13 的性能就不会太令人惊讶，尽管 Framework 将 X7 358H 的持续功率限制设置为相对温和的 30 W（在 Windows 最佳性能预设模式下）和 25 W（在平衡模式下）。 这意味着，在视频编码和游戏等持续占用 CPU 和 GPU 的任务中，Laptop 13 Pro 无法达到与华硕 Zenbook UX8407 相同的高度，部分原因是它使用了 Core Ultra X9 芯片，但主要是因为它具有更高的持续功率限制（55 W）。

Panther Lake 真正帮助 Laptop 13 Pro 脱颖而出的是电池寿命。 在屏幕亮度设置为 200 尼特的 PCMark 10 Modern Office 测试中，Laptop 13 Pro 及其 74 WHr 电池仅持续了 18 小时多一点，远远超过之前任何一款 Framework Laptop 13，并且最终足以彻底消除“电池续航时间平庸到较差”这一笔记本电脑的最大缺点。

我们还对其他 Framework 部件进行了一些有限的测试，以了解 74 WHr 电池在较旧的 Framework 主板上的表现如何，以及如果将 Core Ultra Series 3 主板放入带有 61 WHr 电池的当前 Framework Laptop 13 中，其表现如何。

也许并不令人意外的是，Laptop 13 Pro 的电池续航时间绝大部分都归功于 Panther Lake 芯片和 LPCAMM2 内存。 与 61 WHr Framework 电池搭配使用时，该主板仍能持续约 15 小时 45 分钟。 这意味着升级者可以通过升级主板来大幅延长电池寿命，即使他们不喜欢新的底壳、键盘盖和 74 WHr 电池组合。

当使用新的 74 WHr 电池测试 Ryzen AI 300 版本的 Framework 笔记本电脑主板时，我们的运行时间仅超过 11 小时，而使用 61 WHr 电池的运行时间约为 8.5 小时。 这是一个显着的改进，但它基本上与容量的增加成正比。 如果您仍在使用旧的（且老化的）55 WHr Framework 电池之一，则升级尤其值得追求，但它不如主板升级那么重要。

在错误的时间进行正确的刷新

今年，Framework 异乎寻常地公开了其零部件的困境，部分原因是该公司的运营一直比其他个人电脑制造商更加透明，部分原因是为了平息对其不断涨价的批评。

不幸的事实是，这同时是 Framework 有史以来最好、最有趣的主板升级，也是由于 RAM 危机和其他组件短缺而定价如此之高，以至于通常很难让任何类型的购买有意义。 Framework 网站上一根 32GB 的 LPCAMM2 售价为 800 美元；售后市场上为数不多的一款售价 700 美元。 即使按照内存短缺的标准来看，这也是一个很高的要价。

对于寻求升级的现有 Framework 笔记本电脑用户来说，一些新部件更容易证明其合理性，这是 Framework 可以夸耀的一件事，而大多数笔记本电脑制造商却无法做到这一点。 它仍然要花费几百美元，但您可以保留现在的规格，并受益于更大的电池和更好的底壳，而价格只是全新机器的一小部分。

对于其他人来说，情况更加模糊。 很难知道当前的零部件短缺将如何解决——未来一两年情况会趋于平衡并且价格会回落，还是您会回顾我们当前糟糕的定价环境并希望在情况变得更糟之前购买一些东西？ 无论哪种方式，您都可以以比这低得多的价格购买优质笔记本电脑，包括实际的 MacBook Pro。

  • 典型框架优点：模块化、可修复、可升级设计；漂亮的屏幕、键盘和触控板；对 Linux 和 Windows 的官方支持。
  • 出色的电池续航时间最终解决了 Framework Laptop 13 的最大缺点之一。
  • CPU 和 GPU 性能的良好平衡。
  • 提高了构建质量。

  • 可定制的端口，但你仍然只能得到其中四个。
